13.7 Molecules, Molecular Properties of Matter and Intermolecular Force Everything is composed of a large number of small identical particles called molecules. The properties of such molecules determine the physical properties of a matter.

Basically, the properties of a matter are of two categories; physical properties (electrical, magnetic, thermal, optical, acoustic, radiological mechanical, etc.), and chemical properties (stability, reactivity, toxicity flammability, etc). Physical properties describe the interaction between matter and energy and are measured in terms of density, temperature; viscosity, surface tension, etc., whereas chemical properties describe the chemical response and interaction. Physical properties explain the rearrangement of molecules whereas chemical properties explain intra-molecular rearrangement. Therefore, generally, less energy is required to bring changes in physical properties than in chemical properties. The intermolecular force of attraction affects and determines the physical behavior of a matter. To understand the physical properties of a matter it is fundamental to understand intermolecular forces.

13.8 Kinetic Molecular Model of Gases According to the kinetic molecular model of a gas, a gas consists of a large number of molecules. Except at absolute zero temperature, molecules are in continuous random motion with all possible velocities. Because of random motion, the molecules collide with each other as well as with the wall of the container. Both the collisions are elastic in nature. During collision molecules transfer momentum to the wall of the container, therefore, according to Newton’s law of motion, the rate of change of momentum results in the force which acts on the wall. Also, the force acting per unit area of the wall gives pressure exerted by the gas in the container.

Since, the diameter of a single gas molecule is very much shorter than the average separation between the molecules, the volume of a single molecule is taken as zero. That is a molecule is supposed to be free to move inside the container. Using this model, different laws of gas ( Charles’s, Boyle’s, etc.) are derived.
